What national data says about the STEM completion gap

A reproducible analysis of U.S. bachelor’s degree completion in STEM fields using public IPEDS data: who finishes, who doesn’t, and where the gaps actually live.
Data analysis · Public dataset · Higher education

What national data says about the STEM completion gap

A reproducible analysis of U.S. bachelor's degree completion in STEM fields using public IPEDS data. We know completion gaps exist. This analysis seeks to explore where the gap opens, who it traps, and what the institutional data can reliabily tell us about why.

  • Public dataset (IPEDS / NCES)
  • Descriptive & longitudinal analysis
  • Equity-stratified outcomes
  • Data wrangling at scale
  • Python · pandas · matplotlib
  • Reproducible reporting (Quarto)

Why this question

I spent years redesigning single STEM gateway courses and watched what shifted when the design changed, and what didn't. That's the view from inside one classroom. The view from outside it at the level of every U.S. degree-granting institution, across almost a decade is what this analysis goes after.

The question: where in the STEM bachelor's degree pipeline does the equity gap sit, and how stable is the pattern across fields and institution types?

A gap reported as a single national number can obscure actionable nuance. A gap broken out by instructional programs (CIP field) and institution sector tells you where action can have impact and where the national average is smoothing informative variation.

The data

All from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), maintained by the National Center for Education Statistics. Public, free, no registration required.

  • Completions (C_A survey) — degree counts by 6-digit CIP code, award level, race/ethnicity, and gender, by institution and year. Bachelor's degrees = AWLEVEL=5, first majors only (MAJORNUM=1).
  • Institutional Characteristics (HD) — sector, Carnegie classification, control type. The grouping variables that make the rest meaningful.

Scope: U.S. Title IV degree-granting institutions. Years: 2013, 2015–2023 (2014 data excluded — file truncated at row 253,038, reducing institution coverage by ~28%; the artifact produced a spurious one-year dip that is not a real trend). STEM definition: NSF STEM CIP crosswalk (2-digit families: 11, 14, 15, 26, 27, 40, 41, 03). Health professions (CIP 51) reported separately — including them substantially shifts the gendered patterns in the data.

~2,440–2,800 institutions per year. ~78,000–84,000 institution × CIP × demographic rows per year after filtering to bachelor's level.

What I expected to find — and what the data said

I wrote the expected pattern before running the analysis. Without that discipline, every result looks obvious in retrospect.

What I expected: overall STEM bachelor's counts rising; Black and Hispanic students underrepresented in STEM relative to their share of all bachelor's degrees; the gap larger and more stable in engineering and physical sciences than in biology or CS; a sector effect showing the gap concentrated at doctoral-granting institutions.

What I found: the first two confirmed, the third partially, the fourth not the way I expected.

Finding 1: The gap is persistent, not closing

The core measure: STEM degrees as a share of each group's total bachelor's degrees earned. If a group earned a total of 500,000 bachelor's degrees in a given year and 75,000 of those are STEM degrees their stem share is calculated as 75,000/500,000 = 15%.

Black students earned 5.7% of their bachelor's degrees in STEM in 2013. By 2023 that was 8.0% — a 2.3 percentage point gain over ten years. White students went from 8.6% to 11.0% over the same period. The gap between Black students' STEM share and White students' STEM share was 2.9 percentage points in 2013 and 3.0 points in 2023. Nearly unchanged across a decade in which both numbers rose substantially.

The gap did not move in a straight line. It widened to 3.6 pp by 2018 as White students' STEM enrollment accelerated faster, then slowly narrowed — reaching 3.0 pp by 2023, nearly back to where it started. Both movements happened while everyone was gaining. The lines are rising together but not converging.

Hispanic students fared better — 7.3% to 9.8% over the decade, and the gap to White students narrowed slightly from 1.3 pp to 1.2 pp. That counts as marginal progress against a persistent structural pattern. Asian students rose from 15.3% to 19.7%, the largest absolute gain of any group and the widest advantage over White students.

2013 2023 pp change gap to White (2023)
Asian 15.3% 19.7% +4.4 +8.7
White 8.6% 11.0% +2.4 —
Hispanic 7.3% 9.8% +2.5 −1.2
Black 5.7% 8.0% +2.3 −3.0

STEM share of each group's bachelor's degrees. pp change = percentage point change, 2013–2023. Gap to White = difference from White STEM share in 2023; negative values indicate below White.

The trend lines are all moving in the same direction across the full decade. That matters: it means overall STEM enrollment is expanding and pulling everyone along. It does not mean the gap is closing. A decade of growth and the four lines are not meaningfully converging.

Finding 2: Who's actually driving the growth

Counts indexed to 2013 = 100 show how each group's STEM bachelor's production grew over the decade.

Hispanic students' STEM bachelor's completions grew 129% between 2013 and 2023, from 28,633 to 65,457 — more than seven times the rate for White students (+18%). Asian students' completions grew 79% (36,136 to 64,708). Black students' completions grew 44% (20,664 to 29,808), outpacing White students substantially but still far behind Hispanic and Asian students' rates.

The growth story for Hispanic students over the full decade is striking. It shows up in the STEM share chart too — the line for Hispanic students has closed more distance on White students than any other group. But the starting base still matters: Hispanic students began at 28,633 STEM degrees in 2013 versus 197,256 for White students. Even after doubling, their share gap to White students has barely moved — from 1.3 pp to 1.2 pp. Scale and share are two different problems.

The growth story for Black students is harder to read. +44% raw growth over ten years sounds substantial, but it's still the slowest absolute share gain of any group against White students. The STEM share gap between Black and White students in 2023 (3.0 pp) is almost identical to 2013 (2.9 pp). The pipeline grew; the gap did not close.

Finding 3: The field-level breakdown is where the national average stops being useful

The aggregated STEM share hides enormous variation. Biology and computer science behave nothing like engineering and physical sciences.

A few things stand out:

Computer science is the wrong kind of outlier. Black students had 10.7% of CS bachelor's in 2013 — the highest of any non-biology STEM field. By 2023 that had dropped to 8.6%, while CS as a whole more than doubled in size (+122%). CS added over 63,000 bachelor's degrees between 2013 and 2023; the share of those going to Black students fell. The field expanded dramatically and Black representation shrank within it — a decade-long pattern, not a blip.

While total CS bachelor's grew 122% over the same period.

Biology is the most diverse major STEM field and has grown more so. Black students (8.0%) and Hispanic students (16.7%) both reach their highest representation in biological sciences by 2023. The Hispanic gain in biology — from 9.7% in 2013 to 16.7% in 2023, a 7.0 pp increase — is the single largest field-level representation gain in the dataset. Biology is also the largest STEM field by degree count (132,558 bachelor's in 2023), making this meaningful at scale.

Engineering made modest progress for Black students and large gains for Hispanic students. Black representation in engineering went from 4.0% in 2013 to 4.3% in 2023 — barely moved while the field added 33,000 annual degrees (+38%). Hispanic representation in engineering went from 9.0% to 14.5%, a 5.5 pp gain in a growing field. Those are two very different trajectories in the same discipline.

Math and statistics is a quiet decline for Black students. Black representation in mathematics and statistics fell from 4.8% in 2013 to 3.5% in 2023. This didn't appear in the earlier 2013–2017 window and is new to the extended data. It's the only field where Black share has declined while the field itself grew.

Hispanic students are gaining across every field. Every field shows Hispanic growth from 2013 to 2023, with the largest gains in biology (+7.0 pp), engineering (+5.5 pp), physical sciences (+6.4 pp), and engineering technologies (+5.8 pp). The breadth of the gain is as notable as the magnitude.

The field-level variation matters for interpreting the national number. "STEM" isn't one pipeline — it's seven substantially different ones, with substantially different representation patterns. An intervention designed for engineering won't transfer directly to biology, and vice versa.

Finding 4: Public vs. private nonprofit — the sector effect is real but consistent

Public institutions show consistently higher STEM shares across all racial/ethnic groups — roughly 1–1.5 percentage points higher than private nonprofit institutions for Black and Hispanic students, a gap that persists across the full 2013–2023 window. At public institutions, Black students' STEM share rose from 6.2% to 9.0% and Hispanic students' from 7.8% to 10.4%. At private nonprofits, Black students' rose from 5.2% to 7.6% and Hispanic students' from 6.9% to 9.6%. Both sectors improved, in roughly parallel tracks.

What this tells you: the equity gap is not primarily a sector artifact. The same pattern shows up whether you're looking at a public research university or a private liberal arts college. The sector difference in absolute STEM share is real, but the gap between groups is similar at both — the structural underrepresentation isn't explained by where students are enrolled.

Where the data stops being able to answer the question

IPEDS is institutional and aggregate. It counts degrees awarded — it doesn't record who left, when, or why. The gap this analysis documents is a completion gap. The attrition gap — at what point in the sequence are students leaving STEM? — requires different data. To get at those questions we need to work from the BPS longitudinal survey and HSLS:09 cohort study.

A few other limits worth naming:

The analysis uses HD2022 institutional characteristics to classify institutions across 2013–2023 data. Control type (public / private) is stable over time; Carnegie classification can shift as institutions grow. Carnegie-stratified results were excluded from the final writeup for this reason.

The 2014 data file truncated during download (EOF error at row 253,038, reducing institution coverage by ~28%) so it was excluded and called out.

The NSF STEM CIP crosswalk is documented and replicable, but "STEM" still does a lot of definitional work. Health professions (CIP 51) are excluded here; including them shifts the gendered patterns substantially and modestly shifts the racial/ethnic patterns as well.

What's next

Institutional outliers. The institutions that close the gap, not matching the pattern, are the analytically interesting ones. A residual analysis would surface them. That's a more targeted analysis than this one, and the one that's actually useful for program design.

Explaining the Math/Statistics decline for Black students. Black representation in mathematics and statistics fell from 4.8% to 3.5% between 2013 and 2023, the only field where the pattern moved backward while the field grew. That result wasn't visible in the 2013–2017 window. What's driving it deserves a closer look: whether it's driven by particular institution types, enrollment shifts within the field, or something else requires finer-grained data.

Persistence vs. completion. IPEDS degrees-awarded data can't tell you when students left. Linking to BPS or HSLS:09 would let you ask: is the gap opening at entry into STEM majors, during gateway courses, or at the point of degree completion? Those are three different problems with three different levers.

Field-level trends for 4-digit CIPs. Computer science (11) contains both traditional CS and information systems. Engineering (14) contains civil, mechanical, electrical, and chemical. The 2-digit aggregation used here is already informative, but 4-digit would show where within these fields the representation patterns are most uneven — and whether the CS decline for Black students is concentrated in particular sub-fields.

COVID effects. The 2020–2021 window is visible as a flattening in some trend lines. Whether the disruption produced any lasting structural shifts in who completes STEM degrees — or whether lines return to pre-pandemic trajectory — will only be readable with additional years of post-2023 data.

The code

Analysis in Python (pandas, matplotlib). Reproducible from raw IPEDS complete data files. The full analysis script is below; the figures directory and processed CSVs are in the repository.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

# STEM CIP families — NSF crosswalk (2-digit)
STEM_CIP_2DIGIT = {
    '03': 'Natural Resources & Conservation',
    '11': 'Computer & Information Sciences',
    '14': 'Engineering',
    '15': 'Engineering Technologies',
    '26': 'Biological & Biomedical Sciences',
    '27': 'Mathematics & Statistics',
    '40': 'Physical Sciences',
    '41': 'Science Technologies',
}

def load_year(year, data_dir):
    """Load one year of IPEDS C_A completions data.
    Filters to AWLEVEL=5 (bachelor's), MAJORNUM=1 (first major).
    Returns df with IS_STEM flag and CIP2 (2-digit) column.
    """
    path = f"{data_dir}/C{year}_A.csv"
    try:
        df = pd.read_csv(path, usecols=NEEDED_COLS, encoding='latin1')
    except Exception:
        # Fall back to Python engine for files with embedded quotes / EOF issues
        df = pd.read_csv(path, usecols=NEEDED_COLS, encoding='latin1',
                         engine='python', on_bad_lines='skip')

    df.columns = df.columns.str.strip()
    df = df[(df['AWLEVEL'] == 5) & (df['MAJORNUM'] == 1)].copy()
    df['CIP2']    = df['CIPCODE'].astype(str).str.split('.').str[0].str.zfill(2)
    df['IS_STEM'] = df['CIP2'].isin(STEM_CIP_2DIGIT.keys())
    df['YEAR']    = year

    # Imputation-suppressed cells are coded as 0 in count columns
    for col in DEMO_COLS:
        df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors='coerce').fillna(0).astype(int)

    return df

# Load 2013, 2015–2017 (2014 excluded: file truncated, ~28% of institutions missing)
frames = [load_year(yr, DATA_DIR) for yr in [2013, 2015, 2016, 2017]]
df = pd.concat(frames, ignore_index=True)

# Merge with HD for institution type
hd = pd.read_csv(f"{DATA_DIR}/HD2022.csv",
                 usecols=['UNITID','CONTROL'], encoding='latin1')
df = df.merge(hd, on='UNITID', how='left')

Data: IPEDS Completions Survey (C_A files) and Institutional Characteristics (HD), downloaded from the NCES complete data files at nces.ed.gov/ipeds/datacenter. All inputs public; no registration required. The full analysis script and figures are in the quarto/work/ directory of this repository.
